how: The hosted LLM played snake through the same question every lane gets ("turn left, go straight or turn right?", from the snake's point of view). 5,659 of its answers were logged.
shad0w trained a table on 3,962 of them in 6.78 s on a CPU: 2 KB.
It was certified on the 1,697 answers it never trained on: it agrees with the LLM on 96.8% of them, and is certified at α = 5% on 100% of moves. Anything below its threshold still goes to the LLM.

Every lane played the same 8 seeded games at each speed. A lane asks for a move; the move lands on the first tick after its answer arrives; until then the snake keeps going straight. 360 recorded games in all (9 speeds); the 6 speeds in the picker above replay here move for move, and every game was re-simulated and checked before publishing.
notes: Recorded on an Apple M5 Pro (15-core CPU, 16-core GPU, 24 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6) on 9 October 2026. The System One models ran in llama.cpp (llama-server 0.6.0) on its 16-core GPU, one game at a time; the hosted LLM's games ran 8 at a time, as a hosted API serves many clients.
Every decision in every lane was a real call, timed as it happened: nothing was reused, even when a circling snake met the same situation again.

shad0w plays like the LLM because it learned from the LLM; the decision models were given the same question with no examples and play their own way, which is why they score lower even without a clock (the no-clock point on the chart). The race is about time; the no-clock point is about play.
Each lane keeps one request in flight at a time (no pipelining), as a simple game loop would. A lane's time per move counts only answers that landed before its game ended.
A hosted System One model (Jev) was not measured: no account with credits was available for this run.
